checks.q: What was the authoritative task?
checks.a: summarize_lending_policy_options (permitted action summarize_lending_policy). Task hash sha256:6f95aaf2adf5b37b11e35805f9bbbb24fdb34f38435590b5042d7c406bdf7b6c (Splunk OBSERVED).

checks.q: Where did task authority originate?
checks.a: The authoritative orchestrator/server task contract (INV-006). Not the LLM. Not the untrusted instruction. Not Splunk. Supporting INV-002: instruction content cannot independently authorize.

checks.q: What was the instruction trust classification?
checks.a: untrusted_instruction on BASELINE, ATTACK, and RETEST.

checks.q: Does untrusted_instruction mean malicious?
checks.a: No. Untrusted != malicious. BASELINE has untrusted_instruction without an unauthorized expansion. It is a trust plane, not exploit proof.

checks.q: What action did the instruction propose?
checks.a: BASELINE: summarize_lending_policy. ATTACK and RETEST: extract_full_policy.

checks.q: Was that proposed action automatically authorized?
checks.a: No. Proposed goal != authorized goal. REQUEST != GRANT. The proposal is influence, not a grant.

checks.q: What did CTRL-GOAL-INTEGRITY-001 decide?
checks.a: BASELINE: OBSERVE untrusted_instruction_cannot_redefine_task. ATTACK: OBSERVE overlay (INTENTIONALLY VULNERABLE LAB PROFILE). RETEST: DENY unauthorized_task_expansion. OBSERVE != ALLOW.

checks.q: Is CTRL-GOAL-INTEGRITY-001 the MCP tool PDP?
checks.a: No. CTRL-GOAL-INTEGRITY-001 evaluates task integrity. CTRL-MCP-001 is the sole tool PDP. An LLM must not be treated as an authorization authority. ML may prioritize investigation; ML must not grant or deny authority.

checks.q: What did CTRL-MCP-001 decide?
checks.a: ALLOW / tool_granted for lookup_policy in BASELINE, ATTACK, and RETEST.

checks.q: Was lookup_policy authorized in ATTACK?
checks.a: Yes. CTRL-MCP-001 ALLOW tool_granted.

checks.q: Was lookup_policy authorized in RETEST?
checks.a: Yes. CTRL-MCP-001 ALLOW tool_granted. MCP did not prevent RETEST.

checks.q: Why does that not make ATTACK and RETEST equivalent?
checks.a: Same authorized tool does not mean same authorized use. ATTACK accepted the expansion (wrong-goal handler 1). RETEST DENYed the expansion and retained summarize (wrong-goal 0, in-task 1). Goal-integrity decision differs; MCP grant does not.

checks.q: What actually executed in ATTACK?
checks.a: extract_full_policy via authorized lookup_policy. Wrong-goal handler 1. In-task handler 0. mcp.started is execution began, not a separate success proof of the expanded goal.

checks.q: What actually executed in RETEST?
checks.a: summarize_lending_policy via authorized lookup_policy. Wrong-goal handler 0. In-task handler 1. The unauthorized goal did not execute. The authorized tool still executed for the original task.

checks.q: What is the authoritative proof the wrong goal did not execute?
checks.a: Runtime wrong-goal handler count = 0 on RETEST (and BASELINE). Splunk corroborates via effective_action in MCP preview + COMPLETE transport. Missing row != proof.

checks.q: Why is DET-MCP-001 0 for RETEST?
checks.a: DET-MCP-001 needs tool DENY then later mcp.started for the same run.id + tool. RETEST goal DENY uses extract_full_policy as gen_ai.tool.name; hop-1 start is lookup_policy. Different tools. 0 rows is CORRECT.

checks.q: Why does DET-MCP-001 silence not mean SAFE?
checks.a: Silence means the DET-MCP-001 predicate did not match. ATTACK executed the wrong goal on an ALLOW path. BASELINE is not SAFE just because the detector is quiet. 0 rows != SAFE.

checks.q: Why is the overlay reason not a production IOC?
checks.a: vulnerable_profile_fail_open:untrusted_instruction_derived_task_authority is a LAB-ONLY VULNERABLE PROFILE MECHANISM. Copying it into production would fire on any system that reused the string and miss real expansions that lack it.

checks.q: Why should a SOC reconstruct task + goal + tool + execution?
checks.a: Tool authorization alone cannot establish that the agent used an authorized tool for an authorized task. TASK, INSTRUCTION, GOAL DECISION, TOOL AUTHORIZATION, and EXECUTION must stay distinguishable.

checks.q: What does AUTHORIZED TOOL != AUTHORIZED USE OF TOOL mean?
checks.a: lookup_policy can be granted and still be the wrong use of that tool. AUTHORIZED TOOL != AUTHORIZED GOAL. The grant answers “may this tool run?” The task contract answers “for what?”

checks.q: Why does an authorized tool not make its result authoritative?
checks.a: CTRL-MCP-001 authorized the invoke (lookup_policy at policy:read). The handler then returned data. INV-002: retrieved content cannot independently authorize privileged actions. Follow-on operations still require a normal authorization check. AUTHORIZED TOOL ≠ AUTHORITATIVE RESULT.

checks.q: What is the difference between provenance and authority?
checks.a: Provenance records where the bytes came from (here: mcp.tool.handler after an authorized call). Content is what those bytes contain. Authority is what is actually permitted by server-owned grant. A result can come from an authorized tool while its content remains non-authoritative data. PROVENANCE ≠ AUTHORITY.

checks.q: What security invariant does MCP-005 test?
checks.a: INV-002 — Data Cannot Grant Authority. MCP-005 begins after a legitimate tool execution and asks whether returned data can alter future authority.

checks.q: Why does the ATTACK follow-on receive ALLOW?
checks.a: Profile vulnerable is INTENTIONALLY VULNERABLE LAB BEHAVIOR. CTRL-MCP-RESULT-001 classifies the MALICIOUS payload, then an overlay labels hop-1 CTRL-MCP-001 ALLOW result_derived_grant for lookup_customer_tier. That ALLOW is result-derived, not a coded server grant. Coded allowed_scope stays policy:read. Preview still lists server_owned_allowed_tools": "lookup_policy".

checks.q: Why does RETEST receive DENY for the same follow-on?
checks.a: Profile defended. Same MALICIOUS fixture (same hash). RESULT-001 stays OBSERVE result_is_data. No overlay. Hop-1 CTRL-MCP-001 DENY tool_not_granted because lookup_customer_tier is not in the server-owned grant. SAME HOSTILE DATA + DIFFERENT SECURITY PROFILE = DIFFERENT AUTHORIZATION OUTCOME.

checks.q: Why is DET-MCP-001 silent during the preferred ATTACK?
checks.a: DET-MCP-001’s invariant is DENY → later mcp.started for the same run/tool. The preferred MCP-005 ATTACK is bad authority → ALLOW → execution. There is no DENY-then-start to match. Silence is expected. It is not a detector failure. No DET-MCP-005 exists.

checks.q: Why does a matching result hash not prove trust?
checks.a: The hash is content identity evidence. ATTACK and RETEST share sha256:f7d67b151741ef7c7efb60242b96f8325996709128293da424f53a547230c358. That supports “same fixture.” It does not make the content trusted and it does not create authority. Hash ≠ trust. Hash ≠ authority.

checks.q: What proves that the RETEST follow-on handler did not execute?
checks.a: Runtime follow-on handler count = 0 is authoritative in this controlled lab. Splunk observed no indexed follow-on execution event. That Splunk absence is corroboration only, and only on a complete copy (RETEST 12=12). Do not say Splunk proved the handler never ran.

checks.q: Why is MCP-005 different from prompt-injection resistance?
checks.a: MCP-005 does not prove the model ignored a malicious instruction. The AI can interpret the data. The data still does not get to create permission. The lab proves an authorization boundary, not prompt-injection resistance.

checks.q: Why would repeated same-tool invocations require stronger correlation?
checks.a: There is no indexed gen_ai.tool.call.id. This lab is tractable because the initial tool (lookup_policy) and follow-on (lookup_customer_tier) differ, plus run.id + sequence + hop.index. Repeated invocations of the same tool in one run would collide under run+tool correlation.

registry_quote.quote: the deputy may possess authority, but that is not proof the caller delegated that authority for this operation.

items: Name the caller, the deputy, and the requested operation from indexed evidence.
Separate delegated authority from ambient deputy authority.
Name INV-001 as the MCP-006 invariant.
Explain why ATTACK CTRL-DELEGATION-001 ALLOW is fail-open, not caller grant.
Explain why RETEST DENYs the same request.
Explain why DET-MCP-001 stays silent on the preferred ATTACK.

idea.text: the deputy may possess authority, but that is not proof the caller delegated that authority for this operation. Splunk is where you hunt a copy of the telemetry. Splunk does not ALLOW or DENY a deputy call.

problem.text: A guided lab: Credit Agent asks Compliance Agent to perform an MCP tool call. CTRL-DELEGATION-001 checks whether the caller actually delegated that operation. CTRL-MCP-001 then checks MCP authorization for the selected policy.

why.text: LAB-MCP-001–005 authorized the acting agent more and more contextually (tool, scope, resource, result data). INV-001 still applies when one agent acts as deputy for another: an agent cannot receive more authority than was explicitly delegated.

boundary.text: text Caller ↓ request Deputy ↓ CTRL-DELEGATION-001 MCP authorize (CTRL-MCP-001) ↓ only if allowed Tool handler

how.text: same caller and deputy as BASELINE. Request: lookup_customer_tier / customer:read / cust-001. Profile vulnerable. testbed.mode=ATTACK.

predict.text: What did CTRL-DELEGATION-001 decide, for which caller/deputy/tool, which authority source was used, and what downstream MCP / execution were indexed?

defend.text: THE DEPUTY MAY BE ALLOWED TO CALL THE TOOL. THE CALLER STILL MUST BE ALLOWED TO ASK. CTRL-DELEGATION-001 evaluates delegated authority. CTRL-MCP-001 evaluates MCP authorization. These controls solve related but different authorization problems. text Caller ↓ Deputy ↓ CTRL-DELEGATION-001 ↓ only if ALLOW CTRL-MCP-001 ↓ only if ALLOW Tool handler Defended RETEST: CTRL-DELEGATION-001 DENY delegated_authority_not_granted. Downstream MCP does not begin. Splunk did not prevent the action. The control did. SERVER AUTHORITY EVIDENCE — LIMITED. No indexed allowed_tools. ---

conclude.text: | Layer | What it can prove | What it cannot prove | |-------|-------------------|----------------------| | Runtime | Handler began or did not (invoke_counts) | Whether Splunk stored a copy | | Local | Sequence and event contract for this process | Downstream HEC/index health | | Export | SDK emit+flush attempted (export.json) | Collector, HEC, or index success. splunk.verified stays false until a search ran | | Splunk indexed | A complete or partial copy arrived (dc(_raw) vs local count) | That the handler never ran, if the copy is incomplete | | Search | How that copy answers Q-MCP- / Q-MCP-DELEGATION | Authorization. Splunk does not ALLOW or DENY | | Detection | No indexed DENY then later mcp.started for that window | The handler never ran. Vulnerable ALLOW is not this detector. The system is not proven secure |

checks.q: Why can the deputy possess more authority than the caller?
checks.a: Compliance Agent is a real MCP principal with its own coded grant (lookup_policy and lookup_customer_tier). Credit Agent is delegated only lookup_policy. Ambient deputy authority is independent of the caller’s grant. DEPUTY AUTHORITY ≠ CALLER AUTHORITY.

checks.q: Why is that dangerous?
checks.a: If the deputy spends ambient authority on a caller request, the caller can cause an operation the caller was not entitled to delegate. That is the confused-deputy failure. INV-001: an agent cannot receive more authority than was explicitly delegated.

checks.q: Why is ambient authority different from delegated authority?
checks.a: Delegated authority is what the caller actually authorized for this request (runtime: lookup_policy). Ambient authority is what the deputy possesses for its own work (runtime includes lookup_customer_tier). Indexed agentsec.delegation.authority.source records which set CTRL-DELEGATION-001 consulted (delegated vs ambient_deputy). Ambient is not delegated.

checks.q: Why isn't downstream MCP ALLOW sufficient proof of caller authorization?
checks.a: CTRL-MCP-001 answers: may the selected MCP policy call this tool at this scope? On ATTACK the selected policy is the deputy’s ambient object, so MCP ALLOW tool_granted is true for Compliance and still false as a Credit grant. CTRL-DELEGATION-001 is the caller/deputy question.

checks.q: Why doesn't execution prove caller authorization?
checks.a: Execution shows the handler began (mcp.started / runtime handler count). ATTACK executed after a vulnerable ALLOW. Successful execution is not proof the caller was authorized to cause it.

checks.q: Why can DET-MCP-001 correctly remain silent?
checks.a: DET-MCP-001’s invariant is DENY → later mcp.started for the same run/tool. The preferred MCP-006 ATTACK is vulnerable ALLOW → execution. There is no DENY-then-start to match. Silence is expected. It is not a detector failure. No DET-MCP-006 exists.

checks.q: What evidence would you need before claiming confused-deputy misuse?
checks.a: At minimum: caller identity, deputy identity, requested operation, indexed authority.source, CTRL-DELEGATION-001 decision/reason, whether downstream MCP ran, and whether execution began. Runtime grant lists remain necessary because there is no indexed allowed_tools. Do not claim confused-deputy misuse from deputy possession alone (BASELINE also possesses ambient lookup_policy with source=delegated).

checks.q: What control should execute before the dangerous operation?
checks.a: CTRL-DELEGATION-001 must run before MCP authorize and before the tool handler. Dangerous operation = handler invoke. Defended RETEST DENYs at delegation (delegated_authority_not_granted) so CTRL-MCP-001 never starts.

checks.q: What proves that the RETEST handler did not execute?
checks.a: Runtime handler count = 0 is authoritative in this controlled lab. Splunk observed no indexed MCP execution event. That Splunk absence is corroboration only, and only on a complete copy (RETEST 6=6). Do not say Splunk proved the handler never ran.

checks.q: Why does an empty Splunk execution table not independently prove prevention?
checks.a: Missing mcp.started can mean DENY, ERROR, schema failure, or export loss. On an incomplete copy it can also mean the start event never arrived. Runtime handler count remains the non-execution proof. Empty table ≠ DENY.

checks.q: Who was the caller and who acted as deputy on the Phase 7C specimens?
checks.a: Caller: acme-agent-credit-002. Deputy: acme-agent-compliance-004. RETEST hop 1 is not indexed (deputy_not_on_indexed_hop1); runtime/manifest still name the deputy.

checks.q: Why would repeated same-tool invocations require stronger correlation?
checks.a: There is no indexed gen_ai.tool.call.id. This lab is one operation per run, correlated by run.id + sequence + hop.index. Repeated invocations of the same tool in one run would collide under run+tool correlation.

idea.text: a tool can be legitimate, its first call can be properly authorized, and its catalog metadata can still contain manipulative content. Metadata is DATA. Metadata may influence what an agent REQUESTS next. Metadata must not determine what authority the server GRANTS next.

problem.text: A guided lab: granted lookup_policy at granted policy:read. The first hop is legitimate. MCP-CATALOG asks whether the tool description can change what the agent may do next.

checks.q: Was the first tool legitimate?
checks.a: Yes. lookup_policy is a granted tool. CTRL-MCP-001 ALLOW tool_granted on BASELINE, ATTACK, and RETEST. Authorized tool ≠ trusted description.

checks.q: Was its catalog metadata treated as authority?
checks.a: No. CTRL-MCP-METADATA-001 is OBSERVE metadata_is_data on A/B/C. OBSERVE ≠ ALLOW. Metadata is untrusted_data with provenance mcp.catalog.snapshot. Provenance ≠ content trust.

checks.q: Did the metadata influence a follow-on request?
checks.a: BASELINE: no. ATTACK and RETEST: yes — a follow-on REQUEST for lookup_customer_tier after the catalog snapshot. REQUEST ≠ GRANT.

checks.q: Who authorized the follow-on?
checks.a: CTRL-MCP-001 on hop 1. ATTACK: vulnerable ALLOW vulnerable_profile_fail_open:metadata_derived_authority. RETEST: DENY tool_not_granted. The description itself was not authorized. Splunk did not authorize. A scanner did not authorize.

checks.q: Did the follow-on handler begin?
checks.a: ATTACK: yes (runtime lookup_customer_tier handler 1, indexed mcp.started / mcp.completed). RETEST: no (runtime handler 0).

checks.q: What changed between ATTACK and RETEST?
checks.a: The security profile, not the metadata. ATTACK hash == RETEST hash sha256:9d0745320ca79852f2fbd7145bf074fcd353e290c18ba16fd02d801f9f3375b1.

checks.q: What evidence is runtime-authoritative?
checks.a: Runtime handler counts. RETEST follow-on handler 0 is the authoritative non-execution proof.

checks.q: What evidence is Splunk corroboration?
checks.a: A COMPLETE Splunk copy (dc(_raw) equals local count) showing no hop-1 mcp.started. Corroboration only. Do not say Splunk proves it was blocked.

checks.q: Why is DET-MCP-001 silent?
checks.a: DET-MCP-001’s invariant is DENY then later mcp.started. Catalog ATTACK is ALLOW-path fail-open. RETEST DENYs with no later start. Silence is a DETECTION GAP, not a detector failure. No DET-MCP-CATALOG.

checks.q: Why would scanner output still not be authorization?
checks.a: Scanner PASS ≠ trusted. Scanner FAIL ≠ runtime DENY. Scanners are not wired into authorization in this lab. Catalog metadata remains data until CTRL-MCP-001 decides.

checks.q: Why can Q-MCP-EXECUTED show an extra OBSERVE row?
checks.a: Q-MCP-EXECUTED groups by run.id + tool. METADATA-001 is also lookup_policy, so the OBSERVE row may inherit mcp.completed. Control-event executed=false is not handler non-execution. Do not teach “metadata executed.”

checks.q: Why must ATTACK/RETEST equality use the hash, not the preview?
checks.a: Preview is bounded and is not the authorization input. Hash is the content fingerprint. Do not correlate ATTACK and RETEST by preview text.

checks.q: Which invariant forbids retrieved/tool-provided content from independently widening authority?
checks.a: INV-002: Retrieved/tool-provided content cannot independently widen authority. Catalog metadata is retrieved/tool-provided content.

registry_quote.quote: This lab teaches one idea: **persisted memory is data that survives into a later run**.

items: Reconstruct WRITE RUN → store → later RECALL RUN → classify → request → authorize → execute as five evidence planes.
Treat write run.id and recall run.id as different identities linked by source_run_id.
Treat provenance as source identity, not trust.
Explain why untrusted_data is classification, not malice.
Explain why ATTACK follow-on ALLOW is a labeled lab overlay, not a server grant.
Explain why RETEST DENYs the same follow-on against the same memory hash.
Treat runtime handler count as authoritative non-execution proof.
Treat missing Splunk mcp.started as corroboration only.

idea.text: persisted memory is data that survives into a later run. Recalled text may influence a REQUEST. It does not become a GRANT. Splunk is where you hunt a copy of the telemetry. Splunk does not ALLOW or DENY a follow-on tool.

problem.text: Write the catalog malicious memory fixture, then recall it on a later run of the intentionally vulnerable ATTACK experiment and observe whether a follow-on lookup_customer_tier request is granted.

why.text: Persisted memory is data (INV-003). It may influence a later REQUEST. It cannot independently mint a GRANT. This ATTACK specimen is labeled vulnerable so you can later RETEST the same memory bytes under defense.

controls.text: The persisted memory bytes in the closed fixture. The attacker wants that later-recalled text treated as authority to call lookup_customer_tier.

boundary.text: STORED != TRUSTED. RECALLED != AUTHORIZED. MEMORY INFLUENCE != AUTHORITY. On this labeled vulnerable experiment the follow-on ungranted tool is ALLOW then executed. That is not universal memory-poisoning bypass.

how.text: Two new run.ids are minted (WRITE then RECALL). Trust remains untrusted_data. CTRL-MEMORY-CONTEXT-001 records OBSERVE. A follow-on request is formed. CTRL-MCP-001 records a labeled fail-open ALLOW. Telemetry is emitted for these executions only.

predict.text: Before you click Launch ATTACK, write: will WRITE persist without granting tools, will CONTEXT-001 OBSERVE or ALLOW, will lookup_customer_tier be requested on the later recall, will CTRL-MCP-001 ALLOW or DENY, and will the handler start?

defend.text: Not: sanitize all memory, block every suspicious string, trust a scanner, ask Splunk, let an LLM decide authority. Memory may influence a REQUEST. Server-owned authorization determines the GRANT. text MALICIOUS MEMORY ↓ RECALL ↓ REQUEST lookup_customer_tier ↓ CTRL-MCP-001 ↓ DENY tool_not_granted ↓ HANDLER DOES NOT START

conclude.text: LOCAL EDUCATIONAL SERVICE when installed locally. On a remote deployment the learner uses the host in the browser address bar. The service is unauthenticated. NOT PRODUCTION AUTHENTICATION. NOT MULTI-TENANT. NOT INTERNET-FACING. CTRL-MEMORY-CONTEXT-001 classifies recalled memory. It does not grant tools. CTRL-MCP-001 is a lab allow-list, not production MCP IAM.

authored.note: Written for learners from the sources named in each block. It is an explanation, not a recording. Facts listed under each block are checked word for word against those sources.

summary.text: An agent can save something it was told into memory so that a later run can use it. This lab asks whether text saved in memory can later give the agent a permission it was never granted. Its one idea: persisted memory is data that survives into a later run. It can influence a request, but it never becomes a grant. The run is a scripted, deterministic sequence, not an AI reasoning on its own.
facts: This lab teaches one idea: persisted memory is data that survives into a later run.
Recalled text may influence a REQUEST. It does not become a GRANT.

glance.label: What the attacker wants
glance.text: The attacker wants text recalled from memory on a later run to be treated as authority to call the lookup_customer_tier tool.
facts: The attacker wants that later-recalled text treated as authority to call lookup_customer_tier.

glance.label: What the attacker controls
glance.text: Only the bytes of one memory entry in the lab's closed fixture. The browser cannot choose the setting, the grants, the memory body or any trust label.
facts: The persisted memory bytes in the closed fixture.
The browser does not choose profile, grants, memory body, or trust labels.

glance.label: Where it gets in
glance.text: Two separate runs. A WRITE run stores the memory entry; a later RECALL run reads it back. Each has its own run id, so one launch in this Academy mints two ids.
facts: WRITE RUN → MEMORY STORE → LATER RECALL RUN → CTRL-MEMORY-CONTEXT-001 → REQUEST → CTRL-MCP-001 → HANDLER.

glance.label: Where the trust boundary is
glance.text: Between the recalled memory and the tool. Recalled text may lead the agent to form a request, but server-owned authorization decides the grant. Persisting something does not make it trusted.
facts: Memory may influence a REQUEST. Server-owned authorization determines the GRANT.
PERSISTED MEMORY != TRUSTED INSTRUCTION

glance.label: How the controls handle it
glance.text: CTRL-MEMORY-CONTEXT-001 only classifies the recalled memory as untrusted data (OBSERVE). CTRL-MCP-001 is the control that decides the follow-on tool request.
facts: CTRL-MEMORY-CONTEXT-001 classifies recalled memory. It does not grant tools.
CTRL-MCP-001 is the tool PDP.

glance.label: Recalled is not obeyed
glance.text: On the vulnerable ATTACK setting the privileged tool ran. In the lab's own words the memory influenced a request and the vulnerable authorization profile granted it; the memory did not grant the tool.
facts: The recalled memory influenced a request. The vulnerable authorization profile granted the request. The memory itself did not grant the tool.

glance.label: What evidence exists
glance.text: Each launch records a write run and a recall run, the memory id and content hash, the recall run's source_run_id, both decisions and the handler count. The handler count is the authoritative record of execution.
facts: Correlation: memory.id + content.hash + source_run_id + destination run.id + agent id + sequence.

checks.q: Where is the trust boundary?

checks.q: Can Splunk DENY the LLM call?

checks.q: Does ALLOW mean the LLM executed?
checks.a: No. ALLOW is a control decision. On BASELINE, Q-CONTROL-DECISION shows executed=false on ALLOW rows. Q-LLM-EXECUTED shows executed=true on llm.started / llm.completed.

checks.q: If Ollama starts then fails, is that prevention?
checks.a: No. That is llm.started + llm.failed, executed=true, outcome=error. It must not be labeled DENY.

checks.q: Why is missing llm. in Splunk not enough to prove prevention?
checks.a: Export can be incomplete. Absence in a partial copy looks like DENY. You need runtime + local completeness, then Splunk as corroboration.

checks.q: What does Q-LLM-AFTER-DENY returning zero rows mean on the defended run?
checks.a: No DENY-then-llm. sequence was observed in that complete Splunk copy. It does not independently prove the runtime never called Ollama.

checks.q: Is the one-row positive control a real AgentSec incident?
checks.a: No. It is SIMULATED | makeresults. It was not indexed (stats count = 0 for that synthetic run.id).

checks.q: Why did stats count by "agentsec.run.id" show 66 and 18?
checks.a: Each unique event has three identical copies of that field (JSON indexed extraction + JSON search-time KV + OTLP attribute). Unique _raw counts stay 22 and 6. Completeness is dc(_raw), not a raw field count. Memorizing 66 is not the security skill — over-counting is the trap.

checks.q: Is a defended Splunk copy with testbed.mode=ATTACK a RETEST?
checks.a: No. Mode is a label. RETEST is the defended ExperimentContext with the same adversarial bytes. Do not infer RETEST from DENY alone.

checks.q: What happens on the labeled vulnerable ATTACK specimen?

checks.q: Why did ATTACK execute?
checks.a: The INTENTIONALLY VULNERABLE LAB PROFILE applied overlay ALLOW vulnerable_profile_fail_open:retrieved_context_derived_authority. Then mcp.started and mcp.completed. Handler 1. Retrieved content influenced the request; the overlay granted it.

checks.q: Why did RETEST not execute?
checks.a: Defended CTRL-MCP-001 DENY tool_not_granted. Handler 0. Same document, same request, different authorization outcome.

checks.q: What proves handler non-execution?
checks.a: Runtime handler count = 0. That is authoritative non-execution in this lab.

checks.q: Why is missing Splunk execution only corroboration?
checks.a: Missing indexed mcp.started can also be a wrong run.id, incomplete copy, or export loss. Only a complete Splunk copy corroborates. Splunk does not prove prevention.

checks.q: Why is DET-MCP-001 empty?
checks.a: DET-MCP-001 needs DENY then later mcp.started. BASELINE had no DENY. ATTACK was ALLOW. RETEST DENY was respected. 0/0/0 is CORRECT.

checks.q: Does DET-MCP-001 silence mean SAFE?
checks.a: No. 0 rows != SAFE. DET-MCP-001 silence is not an all-clear.

checks.q: Why is instruction-like text not a production detector?
checks.a: Policies, runbooks, and training docs are full of imperatives. Instruction-like retrieved text has weak production specificity. AGENT NOTE regex is REJECT as a detector.

checks.q: What telemetry is missing for a stronger detector?
checks.a: A server-owned grant snapshot (allowed_tools) and a stable tool-call identity (gen_ai.tool.call.id). Tenant identity and behavioral baselines are also missing. Until then: TELEMETRY GAP — QUERY NOT DEFENSIBLE for unauthorized execution after retrieval.

checks.q: Why are ATTACK and RETEST comparable?
checks.a: They share document.id, content.hash, provenance, follow-on tool, and requested scope. The discriminator is authorization, then execution.

checks.q: What does INV-002 mean here?
checks.a: INV-002: data cannot grant authority. Retrieved content cannot independently authorize privileged actions.

checks.q: Where could behavioral analytics help later?
checks.a: FUTURE — NOT IMPLEMENTED: rare privileged tool after retrieval, new retrieve→tool sequences, novel provenance, retrieval burst before a sensitive operation, per-agent deviation. Statistical SPL, MLTK, or CDTSM may later rank hunts. ANOMALY != INCIDENT.

checks.q: Can ML grant or deny authority?
checks.a: No. ML may prioritize investigation. ML must not grant or deny authority.
